summary: OWAMP and TWAMP measure delay using timestamped packets. Some implementations insert the timestamp in hardware after the UDP checksum is computed, which breaks the checksum. This experimental RFC defines a checksum complement field to make the checksum right again.

plainLanguage.summary: If you write the time on a letter after sealing it, the seal breaks. This adds a small fix-up note so the seal still works.

questions: when not to use checksum complement
subtitle: Reserving the last two bytes of a measurement packet so hardware timestamping does not break the UDP checksum.

tldr.problem: OWAMP and TWAMP test packets get their accurate timestamp written by hardware as they leave, which changes the payload and so invalidates the UDP checksum in the header.
tldr.mechanism: The last 2 octets of the packet padding are treated as a Checksum Complement, which the timestamping engine adjusts so the existing UDP checksum stays correct.
tldr.outcome: Receivers need no changes, so it interoperates with existing OWAMP and TWAMP implementations. It is Experimental and should not be used in encrypted mode.

facts.label: Location
facts.value: Last 2 octets of the UDP payload

today: RFC 7820 is an Experimental RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its text defines the mechanism only for OWAMP and TWAMP, and points to RFC 7821 for the same idea in NTP.

sections.title: The Timestamp and Checksum Problem
sections.content:
The One-Way Active Measurement Protocol (OWAMP) and the Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP) measure delay and delay variation with timestamped test packets. Where these metrics matter for Service Level Agreements, they must be measured accurately. Some implementations use a hardware timestamping engine that writes the exact transmission time into the Timestamp field as the packet leaves.

Because the packets travel over UDP, changing the payload means the UDP Checksum must be updated. Over IPv4 an entity that cannot update it can only set it to zero, so the receiver ignores it and may accept corrupted packets. Over IPv6 a zero checksum is not allowed except in specific cases, and the use of a zero checksum is generally not recommended.

Since only the Timestamp field changes, the checksum can be updated incrementally. The RFC points to a similar solution for the Precision Time Protocol (PTP) over IPv6, where 2 octets are appended for checksum updates. The same mechanism is defined for NTP in RFC 7821.
sections.plainLanguage: A machine stamps the exact time on each message just as it leaves. That changes the message, so the message's error check no longer matches.

sections.title: The Checksum Complement
sections.content:
The Checksum Complement is a 2-octet field in the last 2 octets of the UDP payload. OWAMP and TWAMP test packets already have a Packet Padding field, and this document uses the last 2 octets of that padding. The field is therefore located at (UDP Length - 2 octets) after the start of the UDP header.

A Checksum Complement MAY be used in OWAMP packets from sender to receiver, in TWAMP packets from sender to reflector, and in TWAMP packets from reflector to sender. It works over both IPv4 and IPv6. A transmitter that includes it MUST include a Packet Padding field long enough to hold it. The padding length is negotiated at session setup through the Padding Length field in the Request-Session or Request-TW-Session message.

An intermediate entity that alters a test packet may update either the UDP Checksum field or the Checksum Complement to keep the checksum correct. Using the complement can be simpler when a packet is processed serially, because the entity updates the timestamp and then the trailing field without going back to the UDP header.
sections.plainLanguage: The last two bytes of the message are left as a blank scratch space. When the time stamp changes the message, the machine writes a matching number in the scratch space so everything adds up again.

sections.title: Padding Length Requirements
sections.content:
When a Checksum Complement is included, the padding MUST be long enough for it. In OWAMP the padding is at least 2 octets. In TWAMP it is at least 29 octets in unauthenticated mode and at least 58 octets in authenticated mode, because reflector packets have a longer header than sender packets (by 27 octets unauthenticated and 56 octets authenticated). With that much padding, both sender and reflector can use a 2-octet complement.

If the TWAMP minimum is not met, the reflector cannot use a Checksum Complement, but the sender still can. When the optional octet reflection or symmetrical size features from RFC 6038 are enabled, both length fields must allow at least 2 octets of padding, and with octet reflection the padding must extend at least 2 octets beyond the reflected octets.

The protocol layer and the timestamping layer are assumed to agree on whether the complement is in use, since both are in the same device. The protocol layer must check that packets have enough padding.
sections.plainLanguage: The scratch space has to fit at the end of the message, so the message must be padded with enough extra room. Replies are a bit bigger on the front, so the sender leaves extra room for them.

sections.title: Authenticated and Encrypted Modes
sections.content:
Receivers need no new behavior. The receiving host verifies the UDP checksum as usual and the OWAMP/TWAMP layer treats the Checksum Complement as part of the padding, so existing implementations that comply with RFC 4656 or RFC 5357 interoperate.

In authenticated mode, the HMAC covers some header fields but not the Timestamp or Packet Padding fields. A Checksum Complement MAY therefore be used there, and an intermediate entity can timestamp the packet and update the complement without touching the HMAC.

In encrypted mode the Timestamp field is encrypted, so the entity would have to store and re-encrypt the packet anyway. The RFC says a Checksum Complement SHOULD NOT be used in encrypted mode, nor when the protocols are secured by other measures such as the IKEv2-derived keys of RFC 7717, since it brings little value.
sections.plainLanguage: If the message is only signed, the signature ignores the time and scratch space, so the trick works. If the message is locked in a box, the box must be reopened anyway, so the trick does not help.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension is meant to be used inside an OWAMP/TWAMP node, between the protocol software and its timestamping engine. It is not meant for intermediate switches and routers between sender and receiver, and any modification of a test packet by them should be treated as a malicious man-in-the-middle attack.

The scheme does not increase the vulnerability to such attacks: an attacker who changes a packet and its Checksum Complement is logically equivalent to one who changes a packet and its UDP Checksum. It is meant for unauthenticated or authenticated mode only.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the machine that sends the message should touch the scratch space. If someone in the middle changes the message, that is treated as tampering.
